title: Operator telemetry batting order (dashboard compaction + tracing draft)
body:
Context and goal:

This is a working draft for an operator-focused telemetry "batting order": a lightweight, prioritized set of metrics, traces, and compact dashboard panels that make oncall and incident triage faster for inference services (hosted + dedicated). The aim is not to catalog every signal, but to provide a minimal pipeline that supports fast, first-look hypotheses and a clear escalation path to richer traces and experiments.

Why a batting order?
- Operators need a small reliable sequence of signals they check first (like a baseball lineup). If the top 5 checks pass, the incident is likely higher layer. If any check fails, it immediately narrows the investigation.
- This doc defines the order, what each signal means, how to interpret common patterns, and short remediation suggestions. Also includes sampling rules and dashboard compaction notes to keep queries cheap.

High-level principles (operator-oriented):
1) First-look signals must be high-cardinality-friendly and cheap to query (pre-aggregated percentiles, small cardinality tags).
2) Trace anchors should be lightweight spans that link to a single detailed trace per suspect request (not full tracing of everything).
3) Dashboards should show a single row of panels per inference path: TTFToken (p50/p95/p99), model-side queueing latency, kv-cache hit rate, request success rate, cost-per-token estimate.
4) Alert thresholds approximate human-perceived failure — start broad, then tighten after 1–2 weeks of ops data.

The batting order (priority checks):
1) Surface perceived latency: time-to-first-token (TTFT) at p95 and p99.
   - Metric name: inference.ttft_ms.percentile
   - Tags: route, model_version, region, tenant_tier
   - Quick check: Is p95 elevated while p50 stable? That implies tail/queueing problems. If p50 also moves, likely a broader capacity or model issue.
   - Remediation: check worker utilization, model warm-start logs, prefetch backlog. For dedicated pools check GPU queue length.

2) Token emission slope (tokens/sec after first token) — helps spot slow generation phases.
   - Metric name: inference.emit_rate_tokens_per_sec.pXX
   - Interpretation: steep drop indicates slow decoding kernels or quantization path regressions.

3) KV-cache warmth / prefix hit ratio (tenant-level and global):
   - Metric name: kvcache.hit_ratio (per-route, per-tenant)
   - Because KV warmness strongly correlates with per-token latency and cost, show: 1) recent hit_ratio (15m), 2) eviction_rate (1h).
   - Cheap approximations: maintain a cardinality-limited heatmap (coarse buckets) instead of full keys.

4) Request success / error breakdown: 5xx category, model inference errors, decoding failures, and tool-call failures.
   - Metric name: inference.request_outcome{ok|5xx|model_error|decode_error}.count
   - Quick triage: spikes in model_error with unchanged TTFT usually indicate model-side failures; 5xx + high TTFT may indicate overloaded services.

5) Cost-per-response (amortized token cost estimate):
   - Metric name: inference.estimated_cost_per_response_usd.avg
   - Use inferred batch sizes, quantization profile, and GPU-minute price to estimate. Useful to detect sudden cost regressions (e.g., unexpected batching changes).

Tracing approach (anchor + sample):
- Do not enable full traces at 100% for high-traffic inference routes. Use an anchor strategy:
  1) Attach a compact span to every request with minimal metadata (request_id, route, model_version, kv_hit boolean, enqueue_ns, first_token_ns).
  2) For trace storage, sample 0.5% uniformly + 100% for requests that hit named error classes or cross critical TLs (TTFT p99 threshold).
  3) When a sampled request is captured, capture additional spans from upstream (API gateway) and GPU worker (model invoke time, kernel path flag).
- Sampling rules should be configurable per route and have feature flags to escalate sampling for rollouts.

Dashboard compaction rules (keep it fast and cheap):
- Limit panels to 1–2 pre-aggregated queries per inference path. Each panel should default to 30m view with a 1m resolution, and allow ad-hoc expansion.
- For percentiles, rely on database-native histograms (p50/p95/p99) rather than raw queries.
- Reduce cardinality by using derived tenant buckets (top-50 tenants + "other") and precomputed model_aliases.
- Use heatmap panels for KV warmth: 10 buckets of warmth percentiles instead of listing keys.

Panel list (compact row for each route):
- Small sparkline: TTFT p50/p95/p99 (30m)
- Gauge: kvcache hit_ratio (15m)
- Bar: request_outcome breakdown (5m)
- Sparkline: tokens/sec slope + rate (30m)
- Cost estimate gauge (1h avg)
- Link button: jump to a trace anchor search for request_id / timeframe

Incident triage flow (operator playbook snippet):
1) Open the route row. Check TTFT p95/p99. If p95 normal, move to request_outcome.
2) If TTFT elevated: check kvcache hit_ratio and worker GPU queue length. Low kv hit -> warmness problem; high queue -> capacity.
3) If errors spike: open recent traces (via anchors). If many traces show 'decode_error' span, escalate to model team.
4) If cost per response increases with no traffic change: suspect batching behavior or quantization fallback—check rollout flags and model_variant routing.

Sampling & retention budget:
- Default sample: 0.5% of successful requests, but 100% of requests crossing severity thresholds. Keep sampled traces for 7 days hot, 30 days cold.
- Aggregate metrics retention: 13 months for monthly reports, but dashboard-level aggregations only 90 days to limit query costs.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- Should we compute a tenant-weighted SLO (gives heavy tenants more influence) or uniform SLOs? Ops prefers weighted for fairness but product wants uniform. (JIRA-INF-4821)
- Level of anchor metadata: how much to include in every compact span before the event becomes too large? Proposal: keep to 10 fields max.
- Cost estimator accuracy: going from heuristics to real chargeback will reduce false positives but increases overhead.

Short-term action items (next 2 weeks):
- [Alice] Prototype a compact panel row for 3 high-traffic routes and run with operators for 1 week.
- [Miguel] Implement anchor span telemetry with kv_hit boolean + enqueue_ns. Add 0.5% sampling rule.
- [Priya] Create a lightweight alert recipe for TTFT p95 increase of 2x over 1h baseline.
- [Samir] Run a query-cost simulation for current dashboards and propose 25% compaction targets.

Notes to self / operator hints:
- When investigating TTFT tails, look for correlation with model_version rollouts and scheduled maintenance windows — many tails look like 'cold model' behavior.
- Eviction spikes often correlate with a background job (embeddings rebuilds, retrieval indexing); maintain a calendar of heavy infra jobs and annotate dashboards.

Appendix: example compact span schema (string list form)
- request_id, route, tenant_bucket, model_version, kv_hit (true|false), enqueue_ms, first_token_ms, tokens_emitted, decode_errors, sample_reason

End of draft. Please comment inline with experiments you run (add timestamped notes). This is intentionally compact — if the team wants a broader metric census we should draft a companion doc for telemetry inventory and query recipes.
